Anomaly Detection.summary: Anomaly detection can use embedding vectors to represent data and identify items that differ from a reference set. OpenAI documents embeddings as useful for anomaly detection, but not a dedicated anomaly-detection API.
Anomaly Detection.explanation: Convert comparable data items into embedding vectors and identify items whose vectors are unusually distant from a reference group. The documentation names anomaly detection as an embedding use case, but does not prescribe a specific detection algorithm or threshold.

example.title: Generate embeddings for anomaly detection
example.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

response = client.embeddings.create(
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    input=["normal event", "unusual event"]
)

vectors = [item.embedding for item in response.data]
print(vectors)
example.explanation: Generate embedding vectors that can then be compared with a distance metric or used by an anomaly-detection system.

interview.question: How can text embeddings be used for anomaly detection?
interview.answer: OpenAI text embedding models accept a text string as input and return an embedding vector. Those vectors provide the representation used by downstream applications such as anomaly detection.

interview.question: What other uses does the documentation list for embeddings?

interview.followUp: Why might one embedding workflow support several tasks? The same semantic vector representation can be compared or grouped differently depending on the downstream objective.

interview.question: What does batch size mean in fine-tuning?

interview.question: How is batch size different from an epoch?
interview.answer: Batch size affects training behavior, not the definition of an epoch. An epoch is one complete pass through the full training dataset, while batch size controls how many examples are handled before each weight update.
interview.followUp: How would you evaluate a change? Compare the fine-tuned model with a fixed evaluation set and change one training setting at a time.

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

    [1.0, 0.0], [0.9, 0.1],
    [0.0, 1.0], [0.1, 0.9],
])

model.fit(embeddings)

interview.answer: It is a table that compares true labels with predicted labels for every class. Correct classifications appear on the diagonal, while off-diagonal cells show class mix-ups.
interview.followUp: How would you use it to improve a classifier? Find large off-diagonal cells, inspect those class definitions and examples, then improve the prompt or retrieved examples for that distinction.

interview.question: How do you read the diagonal?
interview.answer: The diagonal counts correct predictions for each category. The cookbook uses the diagonal pattern to judge whether predictions are concentrated in the correct classes rather than spread across categories.
interview.followUp: What does a weak diagonal suggest? It may indicate poor classification or near-random guessing, so compare it with the baseline and other evaluation metrics.

interview.question: How can a confusion matrix reveal specific classification problems?
interview.answer: Rows correspond to true labels and columns correspond to predicted labels in the cookbook's chart. The axis labels must use the same class order as the matrix values.
interview.followUp: What mistake can produce a misleading chart? Passing labels in a different order from the matrix calculation can make the displayed class names refer to the wrong cells.

keyPoints: Use it to see which categories the classifier confuses.
Diagonal cells count correct predictions for each category.
Off-diagonal cells count predictions assigned to the wrong category.
A strong diagonal pattern indicates that predictions are concentrated on the correct labels.
gotchas: A matrix shows overall errors by class, but it does not explain why a particular ticket was misclassified.
A strong diagonal is useful only when the labels and their order are consistent between the matrix and its axis labels.
A scattered matrix can indicate guessing, so inspect the matrix together with accuracy and per-class metrics.

Constitutional AI.summary: Claude citations attach source locations to answers about supplied documents. PDFs use page locations, while plain text and custom content documents use configurable citation chunks.
Constitutional AI.explanation: The citations feature lets Claude attach source locations to claims derived from provided documents. PDF sources use page locations, while plain text is split into sentences and custom content can define its own citation chunks.

parameters.description: The document content block containing the source to cite.

parameters.description: Turns citation generation on for the document.

parameters.name: source.data
parameters.description: Base64-encoded PDF bytes when using a PDF document source.

parameters.description: The source media type, such as application/pdf.

example.title: Cite a PDF document
example.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
with open("document.pdf", "rb") as f:
    pdf_data = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role":"user","content":[
        {"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":pdf_data},"title":"Document","citations":{"enabled":True}},
        {"type":"text","text":"Summarize the document and cite your claims."}
    ]}]
)
print(response.content)
example.explanation: This sends a PDF as a document block and enables citations for the model's answer.

interview.question: How do you enable citations?
interview.answer: Enable citations on a document content block. Claude then returns citation data with the generated text, including source details such as the document title and location.
interview.followUp: How would you support PDFs? Use a base64-encoded PDF document block with media type application/pdf; returned page locations use one-based page numbers.

interview.question: How are PDF citations represented?
interview.answer: PDF content is cited with page locations. The citation includes the document title and starting and ending page numbers.
interview.followUp: Can an image inside a PDF be cited directly? No. The documentation says that only text content can be cited, even though images are processed.

interview.question: Why use custom content documents?
interview.answer: Custom content documents let the caller choose citation chunks instead of using automatic sentence chunks. This gives control over citation granularity and can treat a whole article as one chunk.
interview.followUp: When is custom content useful? Use it when sentence chunking is a poor fit or when a larger citation unit is easier for users to understand.

keyPoints: The feature works with all current Claude models listed by the documentation.
Plain text documents use sentence-sized citation chunks automatically.
PDF page citations start counting at page one.
Custom content documents let applications choose the citation unit and its size.
gotchas: PDF images can be processed, but citations point only to text.
Plain text citations do not identify fragments smaller than one sentence.

from openai import OpenAI

conversation = client.conversations.create()

response = client.responses.create(

interview.question: How does the Responses API preserve conversation state?
interview.answer: A conversation object stores related conversation items. Pass its ID in a Responses API request to continue the same conversation.
interview.followUp: How can you continue without a conversation object? Use previous_response_id to chain a new response to an earlier one.

interview.question: What is a context window?
interview.answer: The context window is the total token capacity for one request. It can include input, output, and reasoning tokens, depending on the model.
interview.followUp: What should you do when a conversation grows too large? Reduce or summarize the context, and check the model's documented context limit.

interview.question: How do storage and expiration work?
interview.answer: Conversation objects and their items are not subject to the normal 30-day TTL. Responses can be made non-persistent by setting store to false when creating them.
interview.followUp: Does chaining responses reduce billing? No. Earlier input tokens in the chain are still billed as input tokens.

keyPoints: Conversation objects keep their items beyond the standard 30-day response lifetime.
Responses attached to a conversation have their items persisted without that TTL.
A context window limits the total tokens used by one request.
The limit can count input, generated output, and reasoning tokens.
Use the tokenizer tool to estimate the token count of a string before sending it.
gotchas: Using previous_response_id does not avoid input-token charges for earlier turns.
Responses are stored by default, so set store to false when you do not want that behavior.
The context window includes the request's available input, output, and reasoning tokens, so long conversations can exceed it.

Cosine Similarity.summary: Cosine similarity compares embedding vectors by their direction. For OpenAI embeddings, a dot product can calculate it efficiently because the vectors have unit length.
Cosine Similarity.explanation: Cosine similarity measures how closely two embedding vectors point in the same direction. OpenAI embeddings have length 1, so their cosine similarity can be calculated with a dot product, and it gives the same ranking as Euclidean distance.
Cosine Similarity.returns: A similarity score between two embedding vectors; higher scores indicate closer vector directions.

interview.question: What does cosine similarity measure?
interview.answer: Cosine similarity compares the directions of two embedding vectors. A higher score means the vectors are more similar for a search task.
interview.followUp: Why can a dot product be used here? Because OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1.

interview.question: How would you use cosine similarity for semantic search?
interview.answer: Use cosine similarity and rank stored vectors by their score against the query vector. For many vectors, use a vector database to make nearest-neighbor search fast.
interview.followUp: What should you use when the collection becomes large? A vector database is the documented recommendation.

interview.question: What limitation can affect embedding search?
interview.answer: The embedding models described on the page have no knowledge of events after September 2021. This may affect searches involving newer events.
interview.followUp: How could an application handle newer information? Store current text in the searchable data and embed that text for retrieval.

keyPoints: Use cosine similarity to compare an input embedding with stored embeddings.
Because the vectors have unit length, the dot product is a faster way to calculate cosine similarity.
For these normalized embeddings, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance rank results in the same order.
Use a vector database when you need fast nearest-neighbor search across many vectors.
gotchas: Cosine similarity is easiest to compute as a dot product for these embeddings because they are normalized.
Different distance functions usually produce similar results, but the documentation recommends cosine similarity.
The current embedding models do not know about events after September 2021, which can reduce performance in some cases.

useCases.scenario: Transform text into numerical features for downstream machine-learning processing.

interview.question: What does the embeddings API create?
interview.answer: The method accepts text input and a model identifier, then returns embedding vectors in the response data. For multiple inputs, provide an array and read the corresponding vector from each data item.
interview.followUp: How would you embed a batch? Pass an array of strings as input and associate each returned data item with the input at the same position.

interview.question: How do you create an embedding for text?
interview.answer: Use an embedding model such as text-embedding-3-small and provide the text to represent. The returned vector is available from the embedding field of each response item.
interview.followUp: What should change when embedding several texts? Supply multiple strings in the input array and process every returned vector rather than only the first one.

interview.question: Where is the generated vector located in the response?
interview.answer: The API response exposes results through data, and each result contains an embedding vector. The vector can then be used by an application for semantic comparison or retrieval workflows.
interview.followUp: How can the output support retrieval? Store vectors and compare a query vector with stored vectors using a similarity method implemented by the retrieval system.

The documentation uses text-embedding-3-small as a current example model for generating vectors.

Embedding.explanation: The API converts text into a vector of floating-point numbers. Texts with smaller vector distances are more related, while larger distances suggest less related content. You can save vectors in a vector database and compare them for retrieval or other tasks.

interview.question: What is a text embedding?
interview.answer: An embedding is a vector of floating-point numbers that represents text. The distance between two vectors indicates how related their texts are: smaller distances mean stronger relatedness.
interview.followUp: What can embeddings support besides search? They can support clustering, recommendations, anomaly detection, diversity measurement, and classification.

interview.question: How do you create an embedding?
interview.answer: Call the embeddings endpoint with an input string and a model name, such as text-embedding-3-small. The returned vector can then be stored and compared with other vectors.
interview.followUp: How would you process several texts? Pass an array of strings as the input and associate each returned vector with its corresponding input.

interview.question: What does the dimensions parameter do?
interview.answer: text-embedding-3-small produces 1536 dimensions by default, while text-embedding-3-large produces 3072. The dimensions parameter can shorten the vector to reduce storage and compute costs.
interview.followUp: Why might a smaller vector help? It usually needs less memory, storage, and computation, though reducing dimensions can involve a performance trade-off.

keyPoints: Embeddings represent how closely text strings relate to one another.
Search systems can rank stored text by its similarity to a query embedding.
The API returns each embedding as a numeric vector.
Compare vector distances to estimate whether two texts have similar meaning.
The current third-generation models include text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large.
Default vector sizes differ by model: small returns 1536 values and large returns 3072.
gotchas: Usage costs depend on the number of input tokens, not directly on the number of requests.
Use the dimensions parameter when a smaller vector is better for storage, memory, or compute.
Read the vector from the response data; the response also includes fields such as the model and token usage.

embeddings.explanation: The embeddings API transforms input text into a numeric vector intended to preserve aspects of the text's content or meaning. Applications compare these vectors to support semantic similarity tasks such as search, clustering, recommendations, anomaly detection, and classification.

parameters.name: model

example.title: Create a text embedding
example.code:

client = OpenAI()
text = "Semantic search finds related meaning."
result = client.embeddings.create(

    input=text,
)
vector = result.data[0].embedding
print(len(vector))

interview.question: What is an embedding?
interview.answer: An embedding is a vector representation of data that aims to preserve aspects of its content or meaning. Related data tends to produce vectors that are closer together than unrelated data.
interview.followUp: How would you use embeddings for retrieval? Generate vectors for documents and queries, then rank documents by vector similarity.

interview.question: How do you obtain an embedding?
interview.answer: Send the text string and embedding model name to the embeddings endpoint. The response contains the resulting embedding vector for the input.
interview.followUp: What should be persisted for later search? Store document vectors with their source identifiers and metadata, then embed incoming queries with the same model.

interview.question: What problems are embeddings useful for?
interview.answer: Common applications include search, clustering, recommendations, anomaly detection, diversity measurement, and classification. These tasks use relationships between vectors to find similar or unusual text.
interview.followUp: Why is chunking useful for document search? It lets retrieval compare a query with focused portions of a document instead of one vector representing the entire document.

keyPoints: Text embeddings quantify how related text strings are.
Typical applications include semantic search, clustering, recommendations, anomaly detection, diversity measurement, and classification.
The request requires input text and an embedding model name.
Similarity between vectors is useful as a proxy for similarity between the represented data.
Text embedding models accept strings and return vectors.
gotchas: Keep each input within the selected model’s maximum context length; embedding models do not produce output tokens.

interview.question: What is an epoch?
interview.answer: An epoch is one full pass through the training dataset. More epochs can help when the model does not follow examples closely, but too many can reduce diversity.
interview.followUp: How would you choose the next value? Run an evaluation, then increase or decrease epochs by one or two based on the observed behavior.

interview.question: What does the learning rate multiplier control?
interview.answer: The learning rate multiplier changes the size of weight updates. Increase it when the model does not seem to converge.
interview.followUp: Why not always use a large value? Larger updates can be less stable, so change it only when evaluation shows a convergence problem.

interview.question: How should training and test data be divided?
interview.answer: Use a training set for the fine-tuning job and a separate test set for evaluation. Providing both lets the service report statistics for both during training.
interview.followUp: Why create the test set early? It gives a fixed benchmark for comparing the model before and after training.

keyPoints: One epoch means that training has processed every example once.
The learning rate multiplier controls how large each parameter update is.
Batch size is the number of examples used before one weight update.

Training and test statistics help you measure improvement during the job.

Prefer clean, useful examples over a larger dataset with poor examples.
Keep training data separate from test data. Use the test set for evaluation.

interview.question: What is few-shot learning?
interview.answer: Few-shot learning steers a model by placing several input/output demonstrations in the prompt instead of fine-tuning it. The model infers the pattern represented by those demonstrations and uses it for a new input.
interview.followUp: How should the demonstrations be selected? Include a diverse range of possible inputs paired with the desired outputs.

interview.question: Where should few-shot examples be placed?
interview.answer: The examples are usually supplied as part of a developer message in the API request. The new task input is then presented separately for the model to process using the demonstrated pattern.
interview.followUp: Why use a developer message? It is the documented location OpenAI recommends for these examples in an API request.

interview.question: How does few-shot learning differ from fine-tuning?
interview.answer: Few-shot learning uses a handful of examples in the prompt, while fine-tuning trains the model with many more examples than can fit in the prompt. Fine-tuning can therefore improve performance across a wider range of tasks.
interview.followUp: What is the main practical trade-off? Prompt demonstrations avoid training but consume prompt space; fine-tuning requires a training workflow but supports more examples.

keyPoints: A small demonstration set can redirect a general-purpose model toward a task it was not explicitly trained to perform.
The technique works by putting a limited number of paired inputs and desired outputs directly into the prompt.
The model infers the task pattern from the demonstrations rather than receiving a separately trained task-specific model.

gotchas: Use varied demonstrations that cover the possible input patterns; narrow examples may not steer the model reliably across the task.

interview.answer: Create a vector store, upload a file with the File API, and add that file to the vector store. Wait for its indexing status to become completed, then provide the vector store ID in the file_search tool configuration.
interview.followUp: Why does the tool not require a separate search service? File search is hosted by OpenAI, so the API manages tool execution and retrieval when the model selects the tool.

interview.question: How does file search retrieve information?
interview.answer: The model receives file_search as a tool in a Responses API request. If it decides the uploaded knowledge is needed, it calls the hosted tool, which retrieves relevant information using semantic and keyword search.
interview.followUp: What two retrieval methods are documented? The page identifies semantic search and keyword search.

interview.question: What is the supervised fine-tuning workflow?
interview.answer: You prepare JSONL examples, upload the training file with purpose set to fine-tune, and create a job with a base model and training file ID. After training, evaluate the customized model against a holdout set.
interview.followUp: Why keep a holdout set? It gives an independent comparison and helps detect whether the model generalizes beyond its training examples.

interview.question: When should supervised fine-tuning be used?
interview.answer: Use supervised fine-tuning when you can provide correct target responses. The documentation lists classification, nuanced translation, fixed-format generation, and correction of instruction-following failures as suitable tasks.
interview.followUp: When might prompting be enough? If the base model already performs well, prompting and examples may avoid training cost and platform constraints.

interview.question: How do you improve weak fine-tuning results?
interview.answer: Training examples should be accurate, consistent, diverse, and representative of production inputs. Reuse the instructions that worked well before fine-tuning, especially when the dataset has fewer than 100 examples.
interview.followUp: What should change if the model overfits? Inspect the data, reduce epochs, or use an earlier checkpoint if it performs better on evaluation data.

interview.question: What is fine-tuning and what is its basic workflow?
interview.answer: Fine-tuning trains an OpenAI base model on examples representing the inputs and outputs expected in an application. The normal workflow is to collect examples, upload JSONL, create a job, and evaluate the result.
interview.followUp: When should you fine-tune instead of relying only on prompting? Fine-tuning is appropriate when a specific task benefits from learned behavior; evaluation should establish whether it improves representative real-world performance.

interview.question: What data does a fine-tuning job require?
interview.answer: The training dataset is uploaded as a JSONL file, and the file is supplied when creating the fine-tuning job. A validation file is optional and produces periodic validation metrics during training.
interview.followUp: Why keep validation data separate? Overlapping training and validation examples make the validation measurements less representative of generalization.

interview.question: How does reinforcement fine-tuning differ from ordinary fine-tuning?
interview.answer: Reinforcement fine-tuning adds a grader that scores the model's behavior. That score guides the training process, unlike ordinary supervised examples that directly specify desired outputs.
interview.followUp: What extra design problem does reinforcement fine-tuning introduce? The grader must reliably measure the target behavior, or optimization can reward undesirable outputs.

keyPoints: It specializes a base model using examples that reflect the application's expected inputs and outputs.
Begin by assembling representative training examples before starting a job.
The training dataset is uploaded to the platform in JSONL format.
Creating the job starts the model-training process after the data is available.
Reinforcement fine-tuning requires a grader that evaluates model behavior.
Evaluation is a distinct final stage used to judge whether the tuned model meets the task goal.
gotchas: The platform is being phased out: new users cannot access it, while existing users retain limited job-creation access and fine-tuned models remain usable until their base models are deprecated.

Function Calling.summary: Function calling lets OpenAI models request application code or external services through declared function tools. Your application executes the requested calls, returns their outputs, and lets the model continue or answer.
Function Calling.explanation: Function calling lets an OpenAI model request application code or an external service through a declared function schema. The application receives one or more calls, validates and executes their JSON arguments, then submits each result so the model can continue with a final answer or additional calls.
Function Calling.syntax: tools: [{ type: "function", name, description, parameters, strict }]

parameters.name: tools

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Function name selected by the model.

parameters.name: arguments
parameters.description: JSON-encoded arguments generated for the selected function.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.description: JSON Schema describing the function's input arguments.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Whether strict mode is enforced for the function call.

Function Calling.returns: A model response containing zero or more function calls; after tool outputs are submitted, the model returns a final response or additional calls.

interview.question: What is the function-calling flow?
interview.answer: Function calling is a multi-step exchange: provide tools, receive a tool call, execute it in application code, submit the tool output, and receive a final response or more calls. The model selects calls from the available schemas.
interview.followUp: How should a loop handle a response containing several calls? Iterate over all function-call items, execute each safely, submit each corresponding output, and continue until the model returns a non-call response.

interview.question: What belongs in a function definition?
interview.answer: A function definition uses a function type, a name, a usage description, a JSON Schema parameter definition, and a strictness setting. The schema tells the model which arguments the application expects.
interview.followUp: Why include a detailed description? It guides when and how the model should use the function, improving tool selection and argument generation.

interview.question: Who executes a requested function and how is its result returned?
interview.answer: The model does not execute application code itself. Your application parses the model's JSON-encoded arguments, performs the operation, and sends the result back using the tool call's identifier.
interview.followUp: What should production code do before execution? Validate arguments against the expected schema and apply normal authorization, error handling, and side-effect controls.

keyPoints: Treat function calling as an application–model conversation rather than a single completion.
Declare available functions in the request's tools collection.
Run the selected operation in your own application using the generated arguments.
Send execution results back in a follow-up request so the model can incorporate them.
Use the current tools parameter to expose callable functions.
Design response processing for zero, one, or multiple function calls.
gotchas: Handle every response as potentially containing multiple tool calls; do not assume exactly one.
A model-generated call is only a request: your application must run the function and provide its output.

GAN.explanation: Prompt generation creates a clear system prompt from a task or existing prompt. The generated prompt should state the task first, then add details, optional sections, examples, and notes. The documentation also recommends short sentences and multi-turn examples when the prompt needs conversational behavior.

client = OpenAI()

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    input="Write a short product description for a reusable bottle."
)

print(response.output_text)

interview.question: How should a generated system prompt be structured?
interview.answer: Use a concise first instruction, then add details and optional sections. Include examples and notes only when they help define the behavior.
interview.followUp: What should examples contain? They should use placeholders where necessary and reflect realistic multi-turn conversations.

interview.question: What writing style should the prompt request?
interview.answer: Keep sentences short by default. The documentation suggests roughly five to twenty words per sentence, unless the user explicitly asks for very short responses.
interview.followUp: How should a prompt handle an explicit request for short responses? Its examples should use responses of about one to ten words.

interview.question: What input content should prompt generation preserve?
interview.answer: The prompt should preserve important user content, including details, variables, placeholders, guidelines, rubrics, and examples. It should also include constants because they are not treated as prompt injection.
interview.followUp: Why preserve constants? They provide fixed instructions, rules, and examples that belong in the final prompt.

keyPoints: Start with the task instruction. Follow it with details, optional sections, examples, and notes.
Use short sentences by default. This improves readability for conversational prompts.
Prefer direct and specific instructions. Remove vague or empty wording.
When the input is unclear, divide the task into smaller steps.
Preserve useful user-provided material instead of replacing it with generic text.
Include fixed values, rules, rubrics, and examples in the generated prompt.
gotchas: The generated result must contain only the completed system prompt. Do not add an introduction or closing explanation.
Conversation examples should include several user and assistant turns. A single question and answer is not enough.
Short examples should explain how real examples should differ in length or detail. Use placeholders when needed.

interview.followUp: Why should code avoid output[0].content[0].text? The output array can contain tool calls, reasoning data, and other items, so that position is not guaranteed to contain text.

interview.question: Where is generated text stored in a response?
interview.answer: The response stores generated content in its output property. In a simple text request, it commonly contains an assistant message with output_text content.
interview.followUp: How can an application safely obtain text? Use the SDK convenience property when available, or inspect output items by their types before reading message content.

interview.question: What does the model input contain?
interview.answer: The input can be a simple string prompt, such as a request for a short story. The selected model then produces a response that the SDK can expose as text.
interview.followUp: What else can a model response contain? It can include tool calls and reasoning-token data in addition to message text.

The documentation lists supervised, vision, direct preference, and reinforcement fine-tuning as separate methods.

interview.question: What is fine-tuning?
interview.answer: Fine-tuning is a model optimization method. It changes model weights using task examples, rather than relying only on instructions in a prompt.
interview.followUp: How should it fit into development? Treat it as one stage in an optimization cycle, then evaluate the result and iterate.

interview.question: What fine-tuning methods are documented?
interview.answer: The documentation presents several methods: supervised fine-tuning, vision fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement fine-tuning. The training data and desired behavior determine which method fits.
interview.followUp: When is supervised fine-tuning a reasonable starting point? Use it when labeled input and target-output examples describe the behavior you want.

interview.question: Why is evaluation needed after fine-tuning?
interview.answer: Fine-tuning is part of a broader optimization cycle. Evaluation is needed to check whether the tuned model improves the target behavior and does not introduce regressions.
interview.followUp: What should be compared? Compare the tuned model with the base model on a representative evaluation set.

keyPoints: Supervised fine-tuning uses examples with desired outputs to teach a model a target behavior.
Vision fine-tuning is available for tasks that include image inputs.
Direct preference optimization is a documented method for training from preference information.
Reinforcement fine-tuning is another documented optimization method for shaping model behavior.
gotchas: Choose the fine-tuning method that matches the kind of training data and behavior you need.

Hallucination.summary: LLM hallucinations are incorrect answers. They can come from bad or noisy retrieved context, or from the model using correct context incorrectly.
Hallucination.explanation: A hallucination is an incorrect model response. A retrieval system can fail by returning wrong or noisy context, so the model cannot answer correctly or may be led toward an unsupported answer. The model can also receive the right context and still misuse it. Evaluate both retrieval and model behavior, then improve search, context, instructions, examples, or training data.

example.title: Answer from reference text
example.explanation: The instruction supplies reference text and tells the model what to do when the answer is absent.

useCases.title: Improve retrieved context
useCases.scenario: A retrieval-augmented generation system returns unsupported answers.

useCases.title: Improve task behavior
useCases.scenario: A model has the right documents but performs a task inconsistently.

useCases.title: Evaluate answer quality
useCases.scenario: A production assistant must be checked for incorrect outputs.

interview.question: What is a hallucination in an LLM application?
interview.answer: A hallucination is a model answer that is not supported by the available information or is otherwise incorrect. In a retrieval system, it can result from bad context or from the model using good context incorrectly.
interview.followUp: How would you diagnose it? Check retrieval quality first, then check the model's instructions and behavior with the retrieved context.

interview.question: How can retrieval cause hallucinations?
interview.answer: Measure whether retrieval returns the needed information and whether it includes unnecessary noise. Improve search, reduce irrelevant results, or add more useful information to each result.
interview.followUp: What should you change if retrieval is good but answers remain wrong? Improve instructions or examples, and consider fine-tuning for more consistent task behavior.

interview.question: What is a practical way to reduce hallucinations?
interview.answer: Start with a simple prompt and a known expected output. Evaluate the result, identify the failure, and make one targeted change to context, instructions, examples, retrieval, or training data.
interview.followUp: Why evaluate before optimizing? Evaluation shows which part failed, helping you choose between improving context and improving model behavior.

keyPoints: Use evaluation to locate the failure before choosing an optimization.
Improve retrieval so it returns information that can answer the user's question.
Remove irrelevant retrieved content because noise can hide useful facts.
Make each retrieved item more useful by including enough supporting information.
If retrieval is correct but the answer is wrong, improve the prompt and task method.
Use fine-tuning when examples can improve accuracy and consistent task behavior.
gotchas: Wrong or overly large retrieved context can prevent a correct answer and increase hallucinations.
Correct retrieved information does not guarantee correct model behavior.

k-Means.summary: K-means clustering groups embedding vectors into a chosen number of clusters. It can reveal hidden themes in text without labeled training data.
k-Means.explanation: K-means clustering groups embedding vectors by similarity. You place the vectors in a matrix, choose the number of clusters, fit the model, and then read the label assigned to each vector.

parameters.name: n_clusters
parameters.description: The number of clusters to create.

parameters.name: matrix
parameters.description: The matrix of embedding vectors used for fitting.

k-Means.returns: One cluster label for each input embedding vector.

example.title: Cluster embedding vectors
example.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

matrix = np.vstack(df.ada_embedding.values)
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init="k-means++", random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(matrix)
df["Cluster"] = kmeans.labels_
example.explanation: This groups embedding vectors into four clusters and stores each cluster label.

useCases.scenario: Group documents by topic when no topic labels exist.

useCases.title: Analyze review text

useCases.title: Explore embeddings

interview.question: What does k-means clustering do with embeddings?
interview.answer: K-means assigns vectors to a chosen number of groups based on their positions in vector space. The model fits the matrix and returns a label for each input vector.
interview.followUp: How would you choose the number of groups? The page example uses four, but the documentation does not prescribe a universal selection method; compare candidate values and inspect the resulting groups.

interview.question: What data shape does the example use?
interview.answer: The input is a matrix in which each row represents one embedding vector. After fitting, the cluster labels are stored alongside the original records.
interview.followUp: Why keep the labels with the records? This lets you connect each discovered group back to the source text or other metadata.

interview.question: Why use embeddings for clustering?
interview.answer: Embeddings provide semantically meaningful vector representations of text. Clustering these vectors can reveal groups such as related topics or review categories without labeled training data.
interview.followUp: What is a limitation of this approach? A cluster can be mathematically coherent without having a useful business meaning, so its contents need review.

keyPoints: K-means can reveal groups that were not labeled in advance.
The example configures four clusters with `n_clusters=4`.
Stack the embedding values into one NumPy matrix for the model.
Store the resulting label on each original data record.
gotchas: The number of clusters is chosen in advance. If you set it incorrectly, the groups may not match the data.
Clustering does not use labeled examples. You must inspect the resulting groups to understand what they represent.

Learning Rate.summary: A learning-rate multiplier controls the size of parameter updates during fine-tuning. Start with the default, then increase it if the model does not appear to converge.
Learning Rate.explanation: A learning-rate multiplier controls how large each weight update is during fine-tuning. Larger values can make training progress faster, while smaller values make updates slower and may be more stable. Start with the service-selected defaults, then raise the multiplier if training does not seem to converge.

example.title: Set the number of epochs

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(
    training_file="file-abc123",
    model="gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18",
    method={
        "type": "supervised",
        "supervised": {"hyperparameters": {"n_epochs": 2}},
    },
)
print(job.id)
example.explanation: This creates a supervised fine-tuning job and sets the number of training epochs to two.

useCases.title: Increase training progress
useCases.scenario: Training does not appear to converge.

useCases.title: Use the service default
useCases.scenario: Choosing initial fine-tuning settings.

interview.question: What does the learning-rate multiplier control?
interview.answer: The learning-rate multiplier changes the size of updates to the model's learned parameters. A larger value can speed up training, while a smaller value can produce slower but more stable updates.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the model does not seem to converge? Increase the learning-rate multiplier.

interview.question: How should you choose an initial learning-rate multiplier?
interview.answer: Start without specifying the learning-rate multiplier. The service chooses a default based on the training dataset size. Adjust it only after reviewing the training results.
interview.followUp: Why avoid setting it immediately? An unsuitable value can make training less stable or prevent useful progress.

interview.question: How does learning rate differ from the other fine-tuning hyperparameters?
interview.answer: The multiplier is one of several fine-tuning hyperparameters. The other listed options are epochs, which count full passes over the dataset, and batch size, which counts examples processed before a weight update.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from batch size? The multiplier changes update magnitude, while batch size changes how many examples are used before each update.

keyPoints: It sets the size of each change to the model's learned parameters.
A larger value may train faster. A smaller value may train more slowly but with greater stability.
Begin with the service's default instead of choosing this value yourself.
If training does not appear to converge, increase the multiplier.
gotchas: Do not set the learning-rate multiplier at first. Use the default selected from the dataset size, then change it when results show a problem.

print(result.results[0].categories)

interview.question: What does the Moderations API return?
interview.answer: The endpoint returns moderation results for submitted content, including a flagged boolean, category labels, and category scores. The application should apply its own policy to decide whether to block, review, or otherwise respond.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a failed moderation operation? Check whether the result is successful before reading scores, then apply an explicit fail-safe policy appropriate to the application.

interview.question: Which input types does moderation support?
interview.answer: The current moderation model handles text and image inputs. It does not classify audio, so audio safety requires a separate control or workflow.
interview.followUp: What if the application receives mixed multimodal content? Moderate each supported text or image input and define a separate policy for unsupported modalities.

interview.question: How can moderation be used with generated content?
interview.answer: Moderation can be performed as a separate endpoint request, or moderation scores can be requested alongside generated content. In the latter case, the model still generates normally, so the application must inspect the scores before displaying or acting on the output.
interview.followUp: What should happen when generated output is flagged? Hold the output from the user-facing path and route it through the application's enforcement or review policy.

keyPoints: Moderation results are signals; your application decides whether to filter content, send it for review, or intervene on an account.
The endpoint does not charge for moderation requests.
Image inputs sent for moderation have a 20 MB size limit.
Use the current omni moderation model for supported text and image requests.

Do not submit known or suspected child sexual abuse material; this API is not a substitute for dedicated child-safety safeguards.

Then describe the action so the model can call it with the right parameters and use the returned data.

interview.question: What are GPT Actions commonly used for in data retrieval?
interview.answer: GPT Actions can retrieve data through an API, a relational database, or a vector database. The API approach calls an external service that supports search and retrieval.
interview.followUp: Which API details should you inspect first? Check its search methods, query inputs, authentication, response structure, and limits.

interview.question: How should you start an API-based retrieval integration?
interview.answer: An API action sends a request to an external provider and returns the provider's data to the GPT. The provider's API documentation determines how the search request must be formed.
interview.followUp: Why can one generic search design fail across providers? Providers expose different search semantics and parameter names.

interview.question: How do API, relational, and vector retrieval differ?
interview.answer: First identify the provider's supported retrieval methods and their inputs. Then model the action around those documented methods instead of assuming a universal search interface.
interview.followUp: What should happen when semantic matching is needed instead? Use a vector database retrieval design that returns relevant text chunks.

Multi-Head Attention.summary: PyTorch's MultiheadAttention jointly attends to information from multiple representation subspaces. It splits the model dimension across parallel heads, combines their outputs, and supports self-attention or cross-attention.
Multi-Head Attention.explanation: MultiheadAttention projects queries, keys, and values into multiple representation subspaces, computes attention independently for each head, concatenates the head outputs, and applies a final projection. With batch_first=True, inputs and outputs use batch, sequence, feature ordering.

For dataset-backed optimization, provide a dataset with the target prompt, an evaluation dataset, at least three rows with responses, and feedback for each row. Run optimization, test the result, add new evaluations, and repeat when needed.

useCases.title: Use focused graders

interview.question: How does the prompt optimizer improve a prompt?
interview.answer: Use the dashboard prompt optimizer to submit a prompt and receive an improved version. With dataset-backed optimization, provide response examples and evaluation feedback so the system can identify changes that improve the target behavior.
interview.followUp: What makes the evaluation useful? Use narrow graders for individual output properties, plus specific Good/Bad annotations and critiques where possible.

interview.question: What data is needed for dataset-backed optimization?
interview.answer: Prepare a dataset containing the prompt and an evaluation dataset. Add at least three rows with responses, and give every row at least one grader result or human annotation.
interview.followUp: What feedback can the optimizer consume? It can use Good/Bad and custom annotations, written output critiques, and grader results.

interview.question: What workflow should follow an optimization run?
interview.answer: Run optimization, inspect and test the new prompt, then generate more outputs and evaluate them. Repeating this cycle can improve the result when the first run is not sufficient.
interview.followUp: How should graders be designed? Make each grader narrowly target a property where the prompt fails instead of combining many unrelated requirements.

The service revises the submitted prompt using current prompting practices before returning the result.
Annotations can include a Good/Bad rating and additional custom columns.
Written critiques in the output_feedback field can guide optimization.
Grader results are another feedback source for the optimizer.
Start an optimization from the Optimize control at the bottom of the prompt pane.

Poor or broad graders can produce weak improvements. Define graders that measure each desired output property precisely.
A dataset-backed optimization requires at least three response rows.

Overfitting.summary: Fine-tuning checkpoints are model versions saved during training. They let you test earlier versions and choose one that performs better before overfitting.
Overfitting.explanation: Fine-tuning checkpoints are model versions saved during training. OpenAI creates one after each training epoch, so you can compare an earlier model with the final model and select a version that generalizes better.

interview.question: What is a fine-tuning checkpoint?
interview.answer: A checkpoint is a model version captured at a particular training step. OpenAI creates a full checkpoint at the end of each training epoch, and you can use it like the final fine-tuned model.
interview.followUp: How would you choose between checkpoints? Compare their validation metrics and test their behavior on examples that were not used for training.

interview.question: Why might an earlier checkpoint be better than the final model?
interview.answer: Checkpoints can help detect overfitting. If quality improves early and later training begins memorizing the dataset, an earlier checkpoint may work better on new inputs.
interview.followUp: What additional evaluation would you run? Use a separate validation or test set and compare task-specific results across checkpoints.

interview.question: How do you find and use a checkpoint?
interview.answer: After the job succeeds, query the checkpoints endpoint with the fine-tuning job ID. The response includes the checkpoint model name and metrics such as validation loss and token accuracy.
interview.followUp: Which checkpoint fields identify its training position? Use step_number for the step and metrics for measurements at that step.

keyPoints: OpenAI creates a complete model checkpoint after every training epoch.
A checkpoint model can be used in the same way as the final fine-tuned model.
After the job succeeds, use its job ID with the checkpoints endpoint to list available checkpoints.
Checkpoint records include metrics that help you judge whether a model is useful.
The step_number field shows when training created the checkpoint.
The metrics field records fine-tuning measurements from the checkpoint's training step.
gotchas: Only checkpoints from the last three epochs are kept, so earlier checkpoints may no longer be available.
A checkpoint can help when training starts to overfit: the final model may memorize the training data instead of learning patterns that generalize.

Prompt Engineering.summary: Prompt engineering designs model instructions and inputs to produce responses that consistently satisfy requirements. Use clear guidance, context, examples, evaluations, and versioned deployment practices to improve reliability.
Prompt Engineering.explanation: Prompt engineering is the deliberate design of model instructions and inputs so responses consistently satisfy a task. You improve prompts by stating the goal clearly, supplying needed context or examples, testing behavior with representative evaluations, and versioning changes as part of deployment.

parameters.name: instructions
parameters.description: High-level behavioral instructions, including tone, goals, and examples of correct responses.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: The task prompt or user input to process.

Prompt Engineering.returns: A model-generated response whose content is evaluated against the prompt's intended requirements.

example.title: Use instructions with the Responses API
example.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5",
    instructions="You are a concise technical tutor. Explain concepts with one example.",
    input="Explain prompt engineering in two sentences."
)
print(response.output_text)
example.explanation: This runnable example separates high-level behavior from the task input when calling the Responses API.

useCases.title: Define model behavior
useCases.scenario: You need consistent behavior, tone, or output constraints across requests.

useCases.title: Evaluate prompt revisions

useCases.title: Version and stage deployments
useCases.scenario: You are releasing prompt changes to a production application.

interview.question: What is prompt engineering, and why does it require testing?
interview.answer: Prompt engineering is writing effective model instructions so the generated content consistently meets requirements. Since generation is non-deterministic, the process combines deliberate design with empirical testing.
interview.followUp: How would you make prompt behavior safer to change? Add representative fixtures, tests, and evaluation checks, then roll changes out through the deployment system with staged controls when needed.

interview.question: How do instructions differ from input in the Responses API?
interview.answer: The Responses API separates high-level behavior in instructions from the task supplied in input. The documentation states that instructions have higher priority than a prompt in input.
interview.followUp: What should be tested when changing instructions? Test representative inputs and expected properties, then compare evaluation results before and after the change.

interview.question: How should prompts be managed in production?
interview.answer: A production prompt should be versioned like application code: keep it in the deployment path, test it against representative fixtures, and evaluate its behavior before release. Pinning model snapshots also helps maintain consistent behavior while prompts evolve.
interview.followUp: What if the model version changes? Re-run the evaluation suite against the new snapshot and review any behavior differences before promotion.

keyPoints: The core activity is crafting instructions that guide the model toward the required result.
Message roles provide a broadly applicable way to structure instructions.
Use the instructions field to define behavior, tone, goals, and examples of correct responses.
Use automated tests and evaluation suites to quantify prompt performance during iteration.
For the Responses API, send the prepared instructions and task input as separate request fields.
Before deploying a prompt revision, establish representative test cases and checks that expose regressions.
Treat prompt updates as deployable configuration and stage them when gradual rollout is appropriate.
gotchas: Do not expect input text to override higher-priority instructions supplied through the Responses API's instructions parameter.
A prompt is not a guarantee of identical output; validate behavior empirically rather than relying on wording alone.

RAG.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant content and adds it to a model prompt before generating an answer. It helps models use proprietary, domain-specific, or newer information.
RAG.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant information at request time and adds it to the model's prompt before generation. The model uses that context to answer questions about proprietary, specialized, or newer information.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description: The model that receives the user input and retrieved context.

parameters.name: input

example.title: Add retrieved context to a prompt
example.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-6-astra",
    input="What is RAG? Use only the context below.\n\nContext: RAG retrieves relevant content and adds it to a model prompt before generating an answer."

useCases.title: Use proprietary data
useCases.scenario: The answer depends on private company documents.

useCases.title: Use newer information
useCases.scenario: The model needs current information that was not in its training data.

useCases.title: Ground answers in chosen sources

interview.question: What is RAG, and how does it work?
interview.answer: RAG means retrieval-augmented generation. The application first finds relevant content, then adds it to the prompt, and finally asks the model to generate an answer using that content.
interview.followUp: What should you evaluate first? Check whether retrieval returns the right, focused context before changing the model behavior.

interview.question: When should you use RAG?
interview.answer: Use RAG when the model needs proprietary data, domain-specific information, or current information that may not be in its training data. It can also constrain answers to selected resources.
interview.followUp: Why might RAG reduce quality? Irrelevant or excessive retrieved text can add noise and confuse the model.

interview.question: How do you improve a RAG system?
interview.answer: A RAG system can fail in retrieval or generation. Improve retrieval by returning better results, reducing noise, or adding more useful information to each result; then evaluate whether the model uses the context correctly.
interview.followUp: How can you isolate the failure? Test retrieval quality separately from answer quality using representative questions and expected results.

keyPoints: Use RAG to provide domain-specific context that the model does not already have.
RAG can provide proprietary or otherwise external data.
Retrieval happens at request time, so the application can use changing information.
Improve retrieval by tuning search to return relevant results and reduce noise.
gotchas: Bad retrieval can make the answer impossible because the supplied context is wrong.
Too much unrelated context can hide the useful information and lead to hallucinations.
RAG quality depends on both the knowledge base and the retrieved results.

Recall.summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning improves models on reasoning tasks that have measurable success criteria. A custom grader scores outputs, and the model learns to produce higher-scoring answers.
Recall.explanation: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) improves a model for tasks that need complex reasoning. You provide training examples and a grader that scores each answer. The model learns from these scores, so clear success rules and reliable grading are needed.
Recall.returns: A grader returns a numeric score that measures how well a generated answer matches the task's success criteria.

example.title: Simple RFT grader
example.explanation: A grader compares the model output with a reference answer and returns a score.

useCases.title: Structured information extraction
useCases.scenario: Extract facts, entities, codes, citations, or metrics from unstructured input into a defined schema.

useCases.title: Schedule management
useCases.scenario: Create, update, delete, classify, and check conflicts for calendar items from messy schedule data.

useCases.title: Engineering-rule application
useCases.scenario: Choose which optional signals or wiring connections should be applied in chip-design verification.

useCases.title: Legal fact extraction
useCases.scenario: Extract legal facts from documents and return structured answers.

interview.question: When should reinforcement fine-tuning be used?
interview.answer: RFT is useful when a task needs reasoning and can be scored with a grader. The grader gives feedback based on how well each generated answer meets the target.
interview.followUp: What makes a task a poor fit? A task is a poor fit when success cannot be measured reliably or when the grader does not reflect the real objective.

interview.question: How should an RFT grader measure quality?
interview.answer: Use a task-specific grader. Depending on the output, it can measure exact correctness, structured fields, span-level F1, fuzzy text similarity, or numeric accuracy.
interview.followUp: How would you grade extracted entities? Compare predicted and expected entities with precision, recall, and F1, while handling duplicates consistently.

interview.question: What results can RFT provide?
interview.answer: RFT can improve difficult structured tasks after prompting or supervised fine-tuning is not good enough. The documentation reports improvements for extraction, scheduling, verification, and tax analysis.
interview.followUp: What should you inspect after training? Check both the overall score and difficult scenarios, then verify that the model is not exploiting weaknesses in the grader.

keyPoints: RFT can train models to extract facts or entities from unstructured text into a fixed schema such as JSON.
Extraction works better with continuous scores rather than only pass or fail results.
Useful grader metrics include span F1, fuzzy text matching, and numeric accuracy.
The Milo scheduling example improved average correctness from 0.86 to 0.91.
The Harvey legal extraction example reported a 20% F1-score increase after RFT.
A tuned model can match or exceed a larger baseline while serving responses faster.
gotchas: A vague grader can teach the model the wrong behavior. Define clear success rules and detailed scoring criteria.
Extraction or selection tasks may contain many optional items. The grader must distinguish applicable items from items that should be ignored.

Reinforcement Learning.summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning trains a model with rewards from a custom grader. It samples answers, scores them, and updates the model to favor higher-scoring answers.
Reinforcement Learning.explanation: For each training prompt, the platform generates several candidate answers. A custom grader scores them, and a policy-gradient update makes higher-scoring answers more likely in later training rounds.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description: The base model to fine-tune; the documentation example uses an o4-mini model.

parameters.name: training_file
parameters.description: The uploaded file containing the training data.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Selects reinforcement fine-tuning as the training method.

Reinforcement Learning.returns: A fine-tuning job object with an identifier and job status.

example.title: Create an RFT job
example.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(
    model="o4-mini-2025-04-16",
    training_file="file-TRAINING_FILE_ID",
    method={"type": "reinforcement"},
)
print(job.id)
example.explanation: This creates a reinforcement fine-tuning job for an o4-mini model. Replace the file ID with an uploaded training file.

useCases.title: Security policy review
useCases.scenario: A model must answer questions using company security policies and follow a required JSON structure.

useCases.title: Custom quality optimization
useCases.scenario: A task needs optimization for a measurable quality signal such as accuracy, style, or safety.

interview.question: How does reinforcement fine-tuning work?
interview.answer: RFT trains a model with feedback from a custom grader. The platform samples multiple answers, scores them, and updates the model toward higher-scoring outputs.
interview.followUp: What makes a grader useful? It should measure the task's real goal and give little reward to lucky guesses or incorrect reasoning.

interview.question: What is the role of the custom grader?
interview.answer: The grader defines the reward signal. Its scores determine which sampled answers become more likely during policy-gradient updates.
interview.followUp: What happens if the grader rewards a shortcut? The model can learn that shortcut, so the task and grader must be designed to make guessing difficult.

interview.question: Which models support RFT?
interview.answer: The documentation says RFT is available only for o-series reasoning models and currently only for o4-mini. Other models should not be assumed to support this method.
interview.followUp: How should model support be checked before starting? Check the current model documentation and fine-tuning support for the selected model.

keyPoints: Reinforcement learning improves behavior through actions, feedback, and repeated adjustment.
For each training prompt, the platform evaluates several candidate answers with the custom grader.
Training uses policy-gradient updates to increase the chance of outputs that receive better rewards.
RFT repeats sampling, grading, and updating across the training data and epochs.
A grader can represent task goals such as accuracy, writing style, safety, or another measurable property.
gotchas: Do not design the task so that a lucky guess can earn a high reward. The reward should depend on the quality of the reasoning or answer.
RFT is limited to o-series reasoning models and, at the time of the documentation, only o4-mini supports it.

interview.question: How do you create a basic text response?
interview.answer: Call responses.create with a model and input. The returned object contains generated output, and the SDK provides output_text for convenient text access.
interview.followUp: How would you handle structured results? Use the Responses API's structured-output capability and consume the response according to the declared schema.

interview.question: Why choose the Responses API instead of Chat Completions?
interview.answer: Responses is intended for direct model requests and supports text, image, audio, tools, and stateful interactions. The API returns output items rather than only a single text field.
interview.followUp: What changes for tool use? Attach the relevant tool and explicitly process the returned tool-call output before continuing the interaction.

interview.question: What are the supported ways to call Responses?
interview.answer: Use the official SDK or call the HTTP endpoint directly. SDK usage requires a client, a model, and input; HTTP requests target the Responses endpoint with bearer authentication.
interview.followUp: What should be reviewed before deployment? Check authentication, errors, rate limits, and request-ID logging in the API reference.

keyPoints: Use Responses as the main entry point for direct model calls that combine generation with structured data, tools, or multimodal inputs.

Structured Outputs are suitable when downstream code needs model results constrained by a JSON schema.

Do not begin new text-generation integrations with the older Chat Completions API when Responses is appropriate.
Prefer Responses for reasoning models to obtain the documented performance and intelligence benefits.

RLHF.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) uses human rankings of model outputs to train a pretrained language model toward preferred behavior. It helps models follow instructions and act more like chatbots.
RLHF.explanation: RLHF trains a pretrained language model to produce behavior that better matches human preferences. People rank two or more example outputs, and reinforcement learning shifts the model toward outputs like those ranked higher.

example.title: Ranking outputs
example.explanation: This example shows the idea of ranking outputs by a human-provided score.

useCases.title: Instruction following
useCases.scenario: You need a model to follow user instructions more reliably.

useCases.title: Chatbot behavior
useCases.scenario: You want responses to match preferred conversational behavior.

useCases.title: Preference alignment
useCases.scenario: You need to shape model outputs using human judgments.

interview.question: What is RLHF?
interview.answer: RLHF means reinforcement learning from human feedback. Humans rank example outputs, and training encourages the model to produce outputs similar to the higher-ranked examples.
interview.followUp: How does RLHF differ from pretraining? Pretraining learns from large unlabeled text, while RLHF uses preference rankings to shape behavior.

interview.question: What does RLHF add after pretraining?
interview.answer: A pretrained model first learns general language patterns by predicting text. RLHF then uses human preferences to make its responses more useful and better aligned with instructions.
interview.followUp: Why is pretraining not enough? It teaches language patterns but does not directly teach the model which answers people prefer.

interview.question: How does human feedback enter the training process?
interview.answer: Human reviewers compare at least two candidate texts and rank them. Reinforcement learning then increases the model's preference for outputs resembling the better-ranked examples.
interview.followUp: What signal guides the update? The ranking supplies the preference signal used during reinforcement learning.

keyPoints: RLHF aligns a pretrained model's behavior with human preferences.
It can improve instruction following and conversational behavior.
Reviewers compare and rank two or more candidate texts.
Training favors outputs that resemble the examples receiving higher rankings.
The documentation identifies RLHF as part of Claude's training for helpful assistance.
gotchas: Human feedback is based on rankings of multiple example outputs, not just a single preferred answer.
Pretraining alone does not make a model reliable at following instructions; RLHF is one refinement step.

RNN.explanation: GPT Actions can retrieve data from external systems in three main ways: API search, structured queries against relational databases, or semantic searches in vector databases. For an API integration, first inspect the provider's documentation to learn its search methods, filters, authentication, limits, and response format.
RNN.returns: Retrieved information from an external API, relational database, or vector database.

useCases.scenario: Find rows that match fields such as status, date, or customer ID.

interview.question: What kinds of data retrieval can a GPT Action perform?
interview.answer: A GPT Action can retrieve data through an API, a relational database, or a vector database. The integration type determines how the query is formed and how results are returned.
interview.followUp: How would you choose between them? Use an API when the provider owns the data interface, a relational database for structured records, and a vector database for semantic text retrieval.

interview.question: What should you check before integrating a REST API?
interview.answer: Start with the external provider's existing API documentation. Confirm how it searches, what filters it accepts, how authentication works, and what response data it returns.
interview.followUp: Why inspect the provider's documentation first? It defines the provider-specific request and response rules that the action must follow.

interview.question: When should you use a relational database or vector database?
interview.answer: A relational database is suited to structured queries over records. A vector database is suited to finding text chunks by semantic similarity rather than exact keywords.
interview.followUp: What is the main difference between keyword and semantic retrieval? Keyword retrieval matches query terms or provider-defined search rules, while semantic retrieval finds content with related meaning.

keyPoints: Data retrieval is a common use for GPT Actions.
An action can call an API and search using keywords.
Relational databases let an action retrieve records with structured queries.
Vector databases can return text chunks based on semantic similarity.
Many business software providers expose REST APIs for searching and retrieving stored information.

Self-Attention.summary: Self-attention lets sequence positions integrate information from one another. PyTorch’s TransformerEncoderLayer implements this with a feedforward network and exposes multi-head attention configuration.
Self-Attention.explanation: Self-attention lets each position in a sequence combine information from other positions using multi-head attention. In PyTorch, TransformerEncoderLayer packages this self-attention with a feedforward network, normalization, dropout, and residual structure; with batch_first=True, inputs and outputs use batch, sequence, feature order.
Self-Attention.syntax: class torch.nn.modules.transformer.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model, nhead, dim_feedforward=2048, dropout=0.1, activation=<function relu>, layer_norm_eps=1e-05, batch_first=False, norm_first=False, bias=True, device=None, dtype=None)

parameters.name: d_model
parameters.description: Number of expected features in each input element; required.

parameters.name: nhead
parameters.description: Number of heads in the multi-head attention module; required.

parameters.name: dim_feedforward
parameters.description: Feedforward network dimension; default 2048.

parameters.name: dropout
parameters.description: Dropout probability; default 0.1.

parameters.name: activation
parameters.description: Intermediate activation: relu, gelu, or a unary callable; default relu.

parameters.name: layer_norm_eps
parameters.description: Layer-normalization epsilon; default 1e-5.

parameters.name: batch_first
parameters.description: Whether input and output use batch, sequence, feature order; default false.

parameters.name: norm_first
parameters.description: Whether normalization occurs before attention and feedforward operations; default false.

parameters.name: bias
parameters.description: Whether to include bias terms; default true.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Device for module parameters.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Data type for module parameters.

Self-Attention.returns: A tensor with the same sequence-feature shape as the input; with batch_first=True, input and output are (batch, sequence, feature).

example.title: Apply a self-attention encoder layer
example.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
    d_model=8, nhead=2, batch_first=True
)
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
y = layer(x)

interview.question: What is supervised fine-tuning, and when is it useful?

interview.question: What kind of data does supervised fine-tuning use?

interview.followUp: What makes a training example valuable? It should represent the production task and contain a reliable target response that exemplifies the desired behavior.

interview.question: Which problems are good candidates for supervised fine-tuning?

interview.followUp: What should be evaluated after tuning? Compare tuned-model outputs with held-out evaluation examples to verify that the intended behavior improved.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

interview.question: What is t-SNE used for in the embeddings workflow?
interview.answer: t-SNE takes high-dimensional embedding vectors and maps them to two dimensions for visualization. It is useful for inspecting structure in embedding data, but the projection is not the embedding itself.
interview.followUp: Why should similarity evaluation remain in the original space? The documentation recommends cosine similarity for comparing embeddings, while t-SNE is introduced for visualization.

interview.question: Which t-SNE parameters appear in the official example?
interview.answer: The documented configuration sets n_components to 2, uses perplexity 15, initializes randomly, sets learning_rate to 200, and fixes random_state at 42. These settings produce a reproducible two-dimensional projection for the example.
interview.followUp: What should change when the dataset or visualization goal changes? Reconsider the projection parameters and validate the resulting plot rather than treating the example values as universal defaults.

interview.question: What does t-SNE transform?
interview.answer: The input is a matrix created from the embedding column, converted to a NumPy array, and passed to TSNE.fit_transform. The result is a two-dimensional representation of the original embedding rows.
interview.followUp: How can the resulting coordinates be used? Attach them to the corresponding records and plot them, while retaining the source embeddings for actual similarity operations.

keyPoints: The dimensionality of the source vectors depends on the embedding model, so visualization code should not assume a fixed input width.
The workflow explicitly creates a t-SNE model and then transforms the embedding matrix.

Use cosine similarity for embedding relatedness rather than interpreting t-SNE coordinates as the canonical similarity space.
gotchas: t-SNE is a visualization transformation, not a replacement for the original embedding space or its similarity metric.

interview.question: What is a token?
interview.answer: Tokens are chunks of commonly occurring character sequences rather than necessarily whole words. For example, a word may split into multiple tokens, while a short common word may remain one token.
interview.followUp: How would you estimate token usage before making a request? Use a tokenizer for the target model; the English rule of thumb is about four characters or three-quarters of a word per token.

interview.question: How can token count be estimated?
interview.answer: A practical English estimate is approximately four characters or 0.75 words per token. This is only a rough estimate, so exact budgeting should use the tokenizer.
interview.followUp: Why can the estimate be inaccurate? Token boundaries depend on the actual character sequences, including spaces and uncommon text.

interview.question: Why does tokenization matter for API requests?
interview.answer: Token count matters because the input and generated output together must fit the model's maximum context length. Counting tokens helps determine whether a request can fit before sending it.
interview.followUp: What changes for embeddings? Since embeddings models do not produce tokens, only the input must remain below their maximum context length.

interview.question: Describe the tool-calling flow.

interview.question: How does retrieval with a vector database work?
interview.answer: Create embeddings for stored text and for each user query. Search the vector database for nearby vectors, then add the matching text chunks to the model’s context.
interview.followUp: Why use middleware? A middleware API can turn plain-text queries into embeddings and expose a REST endpoint when the database does not provide one.

interview.question: Which similarity measure should you use?
interview.answer: Cosine similarity is the recommended distance measure. OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1, so a dot product produces the same ranking as cosine similarity.
interview.followUp: What changes if vectors are not normalized? The dot product can then favor vectors with larger magnitudes, so cosine similarity and dot-product rankings may differ.

interview.question: When is a vector database useful?

interview.followUp: What should you evaluate? Test retrieval quality and the final model response separately, because adding retrieved context can introduce noise.
